sentences.text: Unlike sprawling reptiles such as crocodiles, this animal possessed an erect stance that gave it locomotor superiority and agility.
The largest known specimen, identified as SMNS 52970, preserves a femur measuring 47.8 cm and a skull approximately 50 cm long.
Paired bony plates on its back are scientifically known as osteoderms.
It exhibited heterodonty, possessing sharp teeth that were laterally compressed and varied in size and shape.
The upper jaw held 30 teeth distributed across the premaxillae and maxillae, while the lower jaw contained 22 teeth.
The name Batrachotomus translates to "frog cutter" in Greek, referencing its predation on the large amphibian Mastodonsaurus.
The first specimens were discovered by fossil collector Johann G. Wegele during a 1977 excavation at the Erfurt Formation.
The genus was formally described by paleontologist David J. Gower twenty-two years after the initial discovery of its fossils.
Fossils remained undescribed until 1999, at which point they were previously referred to by paleontologists as "Kupferzellia" or simply "rauisuchid".
The ecosystem included diverse fauna such as fishes, amphibians like Gerrothorax and Mastodonsaurus, nothosaurs, and the marine reptile Tanystropheus.
Recent analyses classify Batrachotomus as a basal loricatan that is most closely related to the clades containing Crocodylomorpha and Rauisuchidae.
A 2011 revision by Sterling J. Nesbitt suggested that the family Prestosuchidae is non-monophyletic based on comprehensive phylogenetic analysis.
Batrachotomus lived in southern Germany during the Ladinian stage of the Middle Triassic, approximately 242 to 237 million years ago.
It inhabited a swampy region in southern Germany.
The time range for Batrachotomus is recorded as the Ladinian stage, specifically between 239.48 and 237 million years ago.
It was hypothesized by Michael Parrish that Batrachotomus originally belonged to the family Rauisuchidae, though later analyses placed it in Prestosuchidae.
